concepts.title: Maximal Clique
concepts.one_liner: A maximal clique is a clique that cannot include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property.
concepts.content:
A **maximal clique** is a clique that can't include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property. The sets of nodes below form maximal cliques (left), or do not (right):

concepts.motivation_md: In graph theory and graphical models, identifying maximal cliques is essential for understanding the largest possible sets of fully interconnected variables, which often define the factors in a probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - A maximal clique is a clique that cannot be extended by adding another adjacent vertex.

concepts.title: Markov Chain
concepts.one_liner: A Markov chain is a graphical model structure where variables form a linear sequence and satisfy the Markov property.
concepts.content:
In perception problems, we typically have both observed and unobserved variables. A simple **Markov chain** structure consists of observed variables $y_i$ and unobserved variables $x_i$:

(see figure: Same three-node Markov chain of @fig-chain.)

This is a chain because the variables form a linear sequence. It's a Markov chain structure because the hidden variables have the Markov property: conditional on $x_2$, variable $x_3$ is independent of variable $x_1$. The joint probability of all the variables shown here is $p(x_1, x_2, x_3, y_1, y_2, y_3) = \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3)$. Using $p(a,b) = p(a \bigm | b) p(b)$, we can also write the probability of the $x$ variables conditioned on the observations $y$,

$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3 \bigm | y_1, y_2, y_3) = \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) \psi_{1}(y_1, x_1) \psi_{2}(y_2, x_2) \psi_{3}(y_3, x_3).$$

For brevity, we write $p(\mathbf{y})$ for $p(y_1, y_2, y_3)$. Thus, to form the conditional distribution, within a normalization factor, we simply include the observed variable values into the joint probability. For vision applications, we often use such Markov chain structures to describe events over time.
concepts.motivation_md: Markov chains are used to model sequences where the future state depends only on the current state, making them ideal for describing temporal events or linear dependencies in computer vision.
concepts.recap_md: - Variables in a Markov chain form a linear sequence where hidden variables satisfy the Markov property.

concepts.title: Markov Random Field (MRF)
concepts.one_liner: A Markov random field (MRF) is a two-dimensional graphical structure used to capture spatial relationships between variables.
concepts.content:
To capture relationships over space, a two-dimensional (2D) structure is useful, called a **Markov random field** (MRF):

(see figure: Two-dimensional Markov random field.)

Then the joint probability over all the variables factorizes into this product:

$$p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{p(\mathbf{y})} \prod_{(i,j)} \phi_{ij}(x_i, x_j) \prod_i \psi_i(x_i, y_i),$$

where the first product is over all spatial neighbors $i$ and $j$, and the second product is over all nodes $i$. An example of how Markov random field models are applied to images is depicted in (see figure: A low-resolution photograph of a tree branch with green leaves against a gray background. A small rectangular red box highlights a specific region of the image, likely to illustrate a local...), which shows a small image region and its context. (see figure: A grid of nodes representing pixels in an image, connected in a Markov Random Field (MRF) structure. Each node is colored either blue or red, representing a binary segmentation of the image into two...) shows an MRF with each node corresponding to a pixel of the image region. The states of an MRF can be indicator variables of image segment membership for each pixel. The states of a hypothetical most-probable configuration of this MRF are shown as the color of each node in this illustration.
concepts.motivation_md: While Markov chains handle linear sequences, MRFs are designed to model spatial dependencies in 2D data, such as pixel relationships in image segmentation.

concepts.title: Directed Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Directed graphical models describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions.
concepts.content:
In addition to undirected graphical models, another type of graphical model is commonly used. **Directed graphical models** describe factorizations of the joint probability into products of conditional probability distributions. Each node in a directed graph contributes a well-specified factor in the joint probability: the probability of its variable, conditioned on all the variables originating arrows pointing into it. So this graph

(see figure: A directed graphical model with three variables.)

denotes the joint probability,

$$p(x_1, x_2, x_3) = p(x_2) p(x_1 \bigm | x_2) p(x_3 \bigm | x_2)$$

The general rule for writing the joint probability described by a directed graph is this: Each node, $x_n$, contributes the factor $p(x_n \bigm | x_{\Xi})$, where $\Xi$ is the set of nodes with arrows pointing in to node $x_n$. Directed graphical models are often used to describe causal processes.
concepts.motivation_md: Directed graphical models are particularly useful for representing causal relationships and hierarchical dependencies where the direction of influence is known.
concepts.recap_md: - Each node contributes a conditional probability factor based on its parent nodes.

slots.key_passage: - Each node contributes a conditional probability factor based on its parent nodes.

concepts.title: Likelihood Term
concepts.one_liner: The likelihood term $p(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.content: The **likelihood term** $p(\mathbf{y} \bigm | \mathbf{x})$ describes how a rendered scene $\mathbf{x}$ generates observations $\mathbf{y}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The likelihood term is a fundamental component of Bayesian inference, quantifying how well a specific model or scene explains the observed data.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the probability of observations given a specific state or scene.

concepts.title: Prior Probability
concepts.one_liner: The prior probability $p(\mathbf{x})$ tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.content: The **prior probability**, $p(\mathbf{x})$, tells the probability of any given scene $\mathbf{x}$ occurring.
concepts.motivation_md: Priors allow us to incorporate existing knowledge or assumptions about the world into our probabilistic models before any data is observed.
concepts.recap_md: - It represents the probability of a state occurring independently of any observations.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.one_liner: The evidence is the denominator $P(\mathbf{y})$ in Bayes' rule, which is constant with respect to the variables being estimated.
concepts.content: The denominator, $P(\mathbf{y})$, is called the **evidence**. In inference, it is often ignored as it is constant with respect to the variables we seek to estimate, $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: The evidence acts as a normalization constant in Bayes' rule, ensuring that the posterior distribution sums to one.
concepts.recap_md: - The evidence $P(\mathbf{y})$ is the total probability of the observed data.

slots.motivation: The evidence acts as a normalization constant in Bayes' rule, ensuring that the posterior distribution sums to one.

concepts.title: Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) Estimate
concepts.one_liner: The maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate is the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability $p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})$.
concepts.content: Selecting the best estimate $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ requires specifying a penalty for making a wrong guess. If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})$. This is because any other explanation $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ for the observations $\mathbf{y}$ would be less probable. This approach is called the **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate.
concepts.motivation_md: MAP estimation provides a single 'best' guess for an unknown variable by combining observed data with prior knowledge.
concepts.recap_md: - The MAP estimate is the mode of the posterior distribution.

slots.motivation: MAP estimation provides a single 'best' guess for an unknown variable by combining observed data with prior knowledge.
slots.key_passage: - The MAP estimate is the mode of the posterior distribution.

If we penalize all wrong answers equally, the best strategy is to guess the value of $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the posterior probability, $p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})$. This is because any other explanation $\mathbf{\hat{x}}$ for the observations $\mathbf{y}$ would be less probable. This approach is called the **maximum a posteriori** (MAP) estimate.

concepts.title: Minimum Mean Squared Error (MMSE) Estimate
concepts.one_liner: The minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate is the point estimate that minimizes the average squared distance from the correct answer, resulting in the mean of the posterior distribution.
concepts.content:
If the penalty function for an estimate is the squared distance in $\mathbf{x}$, then the point estimate that minimizes the average value of that error is called the **minimum mean squared error** estimate (MMSE). To find this estimate, we seek the $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ that minimizes the squared error, weighted by the probability of each outcome:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \mbox{argmin}_{\tilde{\mathbf{x}}} \int_{\mathbf{x}} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y}) (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}})' (\mathbf{x}-\tilde{\mathbf{x}}) d\mathbf{x}$$

Differentiating with respect to $\mathbf{x}$ to solve for the stationary point, which is the global minimum for this convex function, we find:

$$\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE} = \int_{\mathbf{x}} \mathbf{x} p(\mathbf{x} \bigm | \mathbf{y})  d\mathbf{x}.$$

Thus, the minimum mean squared error estimate, $\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{MMSE}$, is the mean of the posterior distribution. If $\mathbf{x}$ represents a discretized space, then the marginalization integrals over $d\mathbf{x}$ become sums over the corresponding discrete states of $\mathbf{x}$.
concepts.motivation_md: In estimation, we often want to penalize errors based on how far they are from the truth. The MMSE estimate specifically minimizes the expected squared error, providing a mathematically convenient and intuitive estimate that corresponds to the center of mass (mean) of the posterior probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - The MMSE estimate minimizes the expected value of the squared distance between the estimate and the true value.

concepts.title: Marginalization in Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: For discrete variables, the marginal probability at a node is computed by summing the joint probability over the states of all other nodes.
concepts.content:
For the case of discrete variables, we compute the marginal probability at a node by summing over the states at all the other nodes:

$$p\left(x_i \mid \mathbf{y}\right)=\sum_{\lambda_i} \sum_{x_j} p\left(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_i, \ldots, x_N \mid \mathbf{y}\right),$$

where the notation $j \backslash i$ means "all possible values of $j$ except for $j = i$."
concepts.motivation_md: Marginalization allows us to focus on the probability distribution of a specific variable of interest by removing the influence of all other nuisance variables in a complex system.
concepts.recap_md: - Marginalization involves summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the joint distribution over all variables except the one of interest.

slots.motivation: Marginalization allows us to focus on the probability distribution of a specific variable of interest by removing the influence of all other nuisance variables in a complex system.
slots.key_passage: - Marginalization involves summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the joint distribution over all variables except the one of interest.

concepts.title: Messages in Belief Propagation

position.section_title: Simple Example of Inference in a Graphical Model

concepts.one_liner: Messages in belief propagation are partial sums that pass information about node states from one node to another.
concepts.content: The partial sums used in marginalization calculations are named **messages** because they pass information from one node to another. For example, a message from node 3 to node 2 is denoted $m_{32}(x_2) = \sum_{x_3} \phi_{23}(x_2, x_3) m_{63}(x_3)$. Similarly, the message from node 2 to node 1 is $m_{21}(x_1) = \sum_{x_2} \phi_{12}(x_1, x_2) m_{52}(x_2) m_{32}(x_2)$. Note that the messages are always about the states of the node that the message is being sent to; that is, the arguments of the message $m_{ij}$ are the states $x_j$ of node $j$. The algorithm corresponding to these calculations is called **belief propagation**.
concepts.motivation_md: Direct marginalization is computationally expensive. By treating partial sums as 'messages' passed between nodes, we can efficiently compute marginals using local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - Messages represent the summarized influence of a subtree on a specific node.

concepts.title: Derivation of Message-Passing Rule
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation message-passing rule is derived by distributing marginalization sums over a tree-structured network of pairwise potentials.
concepts.content:
This derivation describes belief propagation for graphical models with pairwise potentials $\psi_{ij}(x_j, x_i)$. Extensions to higher-order potentials can be achieved by augmenting node states until only pairwise potentials are required. 

Consider a section of a general network with pairwise potentials as shown in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.). In a network of $N+1$ nodes, we marginalize over nodes $x_1 \ldots x_N$. If we assume the nodes form a tree, we can distribute the marginalization sum past nodes for which the sum is a constant value. 

A **belief propagation message** $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is defined as the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$. By passing the summations over node states through nodes that are constant over those summations, we arrive at a factorization where we can read off the recursive message update rule. As illustrated in (see figure: Example motivating belief propagation update rule. (a) Marginalization of a graph with no loops. (b) Shows how the partial sums at $x_j$ distribute over nodes.), marginalization over the states of all nodes leaving node $j$ (not including node $i$) leads to the belief propagation message passing rule.
concepts.motivation_md: To justify the local update rules of Belief Propagation, we must show they are mathematically equivalent to the global marginalization of the joint probability distribution on a tree.
concepts.recap_md: - The rule is derived by exploiting the distributive law to push summations inside products.

slots.motivation: To justify the local update rules of Belief Propagation, we must show they are mathematically equivalent to the global marginalization of the joint probability distribution on a tree.
slots.key_passage: - The rule is derived by exploiting the distributive law to push summations inside products.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message
concepts.one_liner: A belief propagation message $m_{ij}$ is the sum of probabilities over all states of all nodes in the subtree leaving node $i$ excluding node $j$.
concepts.content: We define a **belief propagation message**: A message $m_{ij}$, from node $i$ to node $j$, is the sum of the probability over all states of all nodes in the subtree that leaves node $i$ and does not include node $j$.
concepts.motivation_md: Defining a message as a sum over a subtree allows the algorithm to recursively aggregate information from distant parts of a graph into local computations.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}$ summarizes all information from the subtree 'behind' node $i$ relative to node $j$.

slots.motivation: Defining a message as a sum over a subtree allows the algorithm to recursively aggregate information from distant parts of a graph into local computations.

concepts.title: Belief Propagation Message Passing Rule
concepts.one_liner: The message from node $j$ to $i$ is computed by multiplying incoming messages (excluding $i$'s) with the pairwise potential and marginalizing over $x_j$.
concepts.content:
To compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

1. Multiply together all messages (independent probabilities) coming in to node $j$, except for the message from node $i$ back to node $j$.
2. Multiply by the pairwise compatibility function $\psi_{ij}(x_i, x_j)$.
3. Marginalize over the variable $x_j$.

These steps are summarized in this equation to compute the message from node $j$ to node $i$:

$$m_{j i}\left(x_i\right)=\sum_{x_j} \psi_{i j}\left(x_i, x_j\right) \prod_{k \in \eta(j) \backslash i} m_{k j}\left(x_j\right)$$

where $\eta(j) \backslash i$ means "the neighbors of node $j$ except for node $i$." (see figure: Pictorial depiction of belief propagation message passing rules of equation (@eq-bpupdate), where $\odot$ indicates elementwise multiplication (i.e., the Hadamard product).) shows this equation in a graphical form. Any local potential functions $\phi_{j}(x_j)$ are treated as an additional message into node $j$, such that $m_{0j}(x_j) = \phi_{j}(x_j)$. For continuous variables, the sum over the states of $x_j$ is replaced by an integral over the domain of $x_j$.
concepts.motivation_md: This rule provides a local, recursive way to compute global marginals. It ensures that information is propagated through the network without redundant 'echoes' from the receiving node.
concepts.recap_md: - To send a message to node $i$, node $j$ aggregates all incoming information except what came from $i$.

slots.motivation: This rule provides a local, recursive way to compute global marginals. It ensures that information is propagated through the network without redundant 'echoes' from the receiving node.
slots.key_passage: - To send a message to node $i$, node $j$ aggregates all incoming information except what came from $i$.

concepts.title: Nosey Neighbor Rule
concepts.one_liner: The 'nosey neighbor rule' describes how BP messages convey a neighbor's belief about a node's internal state based on all other available information.
concepts.content: Belief Propagation (BP) messages are partial sums in the marginalization calculation. The arguments of messages are always the state of the node that the message is going to. BP follows the "nosey neighbor rule" (attributed to Brendan Frey): Every node is a house in some neighborhood. Your nosey neighbor says to you, "Given what I've seen myself and everything I've heard from my neighbors, here's what I think is going on inside your house."
concepts.motivation_md: This metaphor provides an intuitive way to remember that messages are directed and represent a summary of 'external' evidence regarding a specific node's state.
concepts.recap_md: - A message $m_{ij}(x_j)$ is node $i$ telling node $j$ what it believes $j$'s state should be.

concepts.title: Marginal Probability in Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: In a loop-free network, the marginal probability at a node is the product of all incoming messages and its local potential.
concepts.content:
The marginal probability at a node $i$ is the sum over the joint probabilities of all states except those of $x_i$. In a network with no loops, the conditional independence structure ensures that the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of the sum of all states of all nodes in each subtree connected to node $i$. Because probabilities within each subtree are independent when conditioned on node $i$, the marginal probability at node $i$ is the product of all incoming messages:

$$p_{i}(x_i) = \prod_{j\in \eta(i)}  m_{ji}(x_i)$$

(see figure: To compute the marginal probability at node $i$, we multiply together all the incoming messages at that node: $p_{i}$ as another message.)

Note that the local clique potential at node $i$, $\psi_i(x_i)$, is included as one of the messages in the product of all messages into node $i$.
concepts.motivation_md: Once messages have been propagated through a tree, this rule allows for the immediate calculation of the exact marginal distribution for any node using only local information.
concepts.recap_md: - The marginal at a node is found by multiplying all messages arriving at that node.

concepts.title: Message Update Sequence
concepts.one_liner: The belief propagation update rule can be applied whenever all the incoming messages required for an outgoing message are defined.
concepts.content: To find all the messages in a graphical model, we invoke the recursive BP update rule. We can apply the update whenever all the incoming messages in the rule are defined. If there are no incoming messages to a node, such as at the leaf nodes of a tree, then its outgoing message is well-defined. This allows us to start the recursive algorithm. A node can send a message whenever all the incoming messages it needs have been computed. In a graphical model tree, we can compute the outgoing messages from leaf nodes because they have no incoming messages other than from the node to which they are sending a message, which does not enter into that specific outgoing message computation.
concepts.motivation_md: This sequence provides a systematic way to compute marginals in tree-structured graphs by identifying a starting point (the leaves) and a recursive order that ensures all necessary information is available for each computation.

concepts.title: Depth-First Update Schedule
concepts.one_liner: In a depth-first update, messages are passed from the leaves up to an arbitrary root and then back down to the leaves.
concepts.content:
In depth-first update, one node is arbitrarily picked as the root. Messages are then passed from the leaves of the tree (relative to that root node) up to the root, then back down to the leaves. When computing marginals at many nodes, we reuse messages with the BP algorithm. A single message-passing sweep through all the nodes lets us calculate the marginal at any node (using the depth-first update rules to calculate the marginal at the root node). A second sweep from the root node back to all the leaf nodes calculates all the messages needed to find the marginal probability at every node. It takes only twice the number of computations to calculate the incoming messages to every node, and thus the marginal probabilities everywhere, as it does to calculate the incoming messages for the marginal probability at a single node.

concepts.title: Synchronous Parallel Update Schedule
concepts.one_liner: In a parallel update, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received the necessary incoming messages at each turn.
concepts.content:
In parallel update, at each turn, every node sends every outgoing message for which it has received all the necessary incoming messages. Each node sends an outgoing message as soon as it receives the necessary incoming messages.

concepts.title: Disparity
concepts.one_liner: Disparity represents the depth of pixels as the difference in position between left and right camera images.
concepts.content: In graphical models for stereo vision, each unobserved variable represents the unknown depth of a pixel in a scan line. Often, we represent this depth as the **disparity** between the left and right camera images.
concepts.motivation_md: Disparity is a computationally convenient way to represent depth in stereo vision, as it relates directly to the observable shift of objects between two different camera perspectives.

concepts.title: Potts Model
concepts.one_liner: The Potts Model is a compatibility matrix where identical neighboring states have a weight of 1 and different states have a weight of $\delta$.
concepts.content:
The prior probability of any configuration of pixel disparity states is described by setting the compatibility matrices, $\mathbf{\phi}[s_i, s_{i+1}]$, of a Markov chain. The Potts Model defines this compatibility matrix as:

$$\mathbf{\phi}[s_i, s_{i+1}] = 
    \begin{cases}
      1, & \text{if}\ s_i = s_{i+1} \\
      \delta, & \text{otherwise}
    \end{cases}$$

In typical stereo vision examples, a value such as $\delta = 0.001$ is used.
concepts.motivation_md: The Potts Model is used to encourage piecewise constant solutions in image processing, penalizing differences between neighboring pixels to promote smoothness while allowing for occasional sharp transitions.

concepts.title: Loopy Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Loopy belief propagation applies standard BP update rules to graphs with cycles to find approximate marginal probabilities.
concepts.content:
The BP message update rules only provide exact marginals when the network topology is a tree or a chain. For graphs with loops, exact computation depends on the treewidth, which can be intractably large for models like 2D Markov random fields. However, applying message update rules locally remains a useful operation even without global guarantees. This is the **loopy belief propagation algorithm**:

1. Convert the graph to pairwise potentials.
2. Initialize all messages to all ones, or to random values between 0 and 1.
3. Run the belief propagation update rules until convergence.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard BP is only exact on trees, many real-world problems (like image processing) involve loops. Loopy BP provides a practical, though approximate, way to perform inference in these complex graphs.

concepts.title: Treewidth
concepts.one_liner: Treewidth is a graph-theoretic quantity that determines the complexity of exact marginal probability computation in graphs with loops.
concepts.content: The BP message update rules only work to give the exact marginals when the topology of the network is that of a tree or a chain. In general, exact computation of marginal probabilities for graphs with loops depends on a graph-theoretic quantity known as the **treewidth** of the graph.
concepts.motivation_md: Treewidth measures how 'tree-like' a graph is. It is a critical concept because the computational cost of exact inference algorithms grows exponentially with the treewidth of the underlying graphical model.

concepts.title: Bethe Free Energy
concepts.one_liner: Fixed points of the belief propagation algorithm in loopy networks correspond to minima of the Bethe free energy approximation.
concepts.content: In networks with loops, fixed points of the belief propagation algorithm—defined as message configurations where messages do not change with an update—correspond to minima of a well-known approximation from statistical physics known as the Bethe free energy. In practice, the solutions found by the loopy belief propagation algorithm can be quite good.
concepts.motivation_md: Connecting BP to Bethe free energy provides a theoretical foundation for why loopy BP works, framing the algorithm as an optimization process that minimizes an approximation of the true energy of the system.

concepts.title: Max-Product Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: The max-product version of belief propagation replaces the summation in the update rule with an argmax operator to compute a MAP estimate of hidden states.
concepts.content: Instead of summing over the states of other nodes, we are sometimes interested in finding the $\mathbf{x}$ that maximizes the joint probability. The argmax operator passes through constant variables just as the summation sign did. This leads to an alternate version of the BP algorithm where the summation (of multiplying the vector message products by the node compatibility matrix) is replaced with argmax. This is called the max-product version of belief propagation, and it computes a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate of the hidden states.
concepts.motivation_md: While standard belief propagation computes marginal probabilities, we often need to find the single most likely configuration of all hidden states (the MAP estimate).
concepts.recap_md: - The max-product algorithm replaces the summation in the belief propagation update rule with an argmax operator. - This variant is used to compute the MAP estimate of hidden states rather than marginal probabilities.

concepts.title: Computational Complexity of Belief Propagation
concepts.one_liner: Belief propagation enables efficient inference by reducing marginalization cost from exponential to linear in the number of nodes for tree-structured graphs.
concepts.content: Running belief propagation within a tree computes exact marginal probabilities at each node by reusing intermediate sums across different marginalizations and exploiting the structure of the joint probability to perform the computation efficiently. If nothing were known about the joint probability structure, the marginalization cost would grow exponentially with the number of nodes in the network. However, if the graph structure corresponding to the joint probability is known to be a chain or a tree, then the marginalization cost only grows linearly with the number of nodes and is quadratic in the node state dimensions. The belief propagation algorithm enables inference in many large-scale problems.
concepts.motivation_md: Direct marginalization of joint distributions is computationally intractable for large networks because the cost grows exponentially with the number of variables.
concepts.recap_md: - In tree or chain structures, belief propagation reduces the computational cost of marginalization from exponential to linear. - The algorithm achieves efficiency by reusing intermediate sums and exploiting the factorization of the joint probability.

concepts.title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models and neural networks both use graph structures but differ significantly in the meaning of nodes, edges, and their underlying computational goals.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models (PGMs) and neural networks (NNs) share a graph structure with nodes and edges, but these components represent different concepts. In NNs, nodes typically represent real-valued scalar activations, while in PGMs, they represent random variables (scalar or vector, discrete or continuous). Edges in PGMs determine statistical dependencies, whereas in NNs, they define the linear summations passed to the next layer. The primary difference lies in computation: PGMs represent factorized probability distributions to compute probabilities like marginals, while NNs compute results that minimize an expected loss or an energy function. This goal of minimizing loss rather than calculating probabilities allows NNs more general computations at the cost of less interpretable, non-probabilistic outputs.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the distinction between PGMs and NNs helps clarify when to use probabilistic inference versus optimization-based learning for a given problem.
concepts.recap_md: - PGMs represent random variables and statistical dependencies to compute probabilities through message passing. - Neural networks use nodes for activations and edges for weights to minimize a loss function rather than calculating probabilities.

concepts.title: Computation in Neural Networks vs. PGMs

position.section_title: Relationship of Probabilistic Graphical Models to Neural Networks

concepts.one_liner: PGMs compute probabilities through factorized distributions, while neural networks focus on minimizing expected loss or energy functions.
concepts.content: The fundamental difference between PGMs and NNs lies in what they calculate. PGMs represent factorized probability distributions and pass messages that allow for the computation of probabilities, such as the marginal probability at a node. In contrast, NNs compute results that minimize some expected loss or an energy function. This different goal of minimizing an expected loss rather than calculating a probability allows for more general computations by a neural network at the cost of output that may be less modular or less interpretable because they are not probabilities.
concepts.motivation_md: The choice between calculating exact probabilities and optimizing a loss function determines the interpretability and flexibility of the model.
concepts.recap_md: - PGMs focus on calculating probabilities like marginals using factorized distributions. - Neural networks optimize for loss minimization, allowing for more general but less interpretable computations.

concepts.title: Probabilistic Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way to reason about complicated visual situations.
concepts.content: Probabilistic graphical models describe joint probability distributions in a modular way that allows us to reason about the visual world even when we're modeling very complicated situations. These models are useful in vision, where we often need to exploit modularity to make computations tractable.
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling complex joint distributions directly is often computationally impossible; graphical models provide a modular framework to make these calculations tractable.

concepts.title: Undirected Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: An undirected graphical model is a graph with nodes representing variables and line segments representing shared structure in a probability distribution.
concepts.content: A probabilistic graphical model is a graph that describes a class of probability distributions sharing a common structure. The graph has nodes, drawn as circles, indicating the variables of the joint probability. It has edges, drawn as lines connecting nodes to other nodes. In undirected graphical models, the edges are line segments without arrowheads.
concepts.motivation_md: Undirected graphs are used to represent symmetric relationships between variables where no specific causal direction is assumed.

concepts.title: Conditional Independence in Graphical Models
concepts.one_liner: In undirected graphical models, the absence of an edge between nodes indicates that the corresponding variables are conditionally independent.
concepts.content: In undirected graphical models, the edges indicate the conditional independence structure of the nodes of the graph. If there is no edge between two nodes, then the variables described by those nodes are independent, conditioned on the values of intervening nodes in any path between them in the graph. If two nodes do have a line between them, then we cannot assume they are independent.
concepts.motivation_md: Identifying conditional independence allows for the factorization of complex joint distributions, significantly simplifying probabilistic inference.
concepts.recap_md: - Missing edges signify conditional independence between variables.

concepts.title: Hammersley-Clifford Theorem
concepts.one_liner: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem states that a positive joint probability distribution must be a product of functions over the maximal cliques of its graphical model.
concepts.content: The Hammersley-Clifford theorem defines the form the joint probability must have for any given graphical model. It states that a positive probability distribution has the independence structure described by a graphical model if and only if it can be written as a product of functions over the variables of each maximal clique: $$p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_N) = \prod_{x_c \in x_i} \Psi_{c} (x_c),$$ where the product is over all maximal cliques $x_c$ in the graph $x_i$. A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique. A maximal clique is a clique that can't include more nodes of the graph without losing the clique property. [FIGURE:a834d415de54d03b | A maximal clique is the largest possible clique.]
concepts.motivation_md: This theorem provides the mathematical bridge between the visual structure of a graph and the algebraic factorization of its probability distribution.
concepts.recap_md: - Joint probability is the product of functions over maximal cliques.

concepts.title: Clique
concepts.one_liner: A clique is a set of nodes in a graph where every node is connected to every other node in the set.
concepts.content: A clique is any set of nodes where each node is connected to every other node in the clique.
concepts.motivation_md: Cliques are the fundamental building blocks used to define local dependencies and factorize joint distributions in graphical models.

prereq.rationale: This concept explains the specific semantic meaning of edges (and their absence) within the undirected graphical model framework.
Directed graphical models are a specific implementation of the broader probabilistic graphical modeling framework.
The factorization of the joint probability into conditional distributions in a directed model is a direct representation of conditional independence assumptions.
The likelihood term describes the generative process from scene to observation, often modeled as a directed relationship in graphical models.
The evidence is the marginalization of the product of the likelihood and the prior over all possible scene states.
The evidence term $P(y)$ is calculated by integrating the product of the likelihood and the prior probability.
The MAP estimate maximizes the posterior, which is proportional to the product of the likelihood and the prior.
The MAP estimate incorporates the prior probability $p(x)$ to find the most probable scene given the observations.
The MMSE estimate is the mean of the posterior distribution, which depends directly on the likelihood term.
The MMSE estimate requires the full posterior distribution, which is formed using the prior probability.
Marginalization is a fundamental operation used to perform inference on nodes within a probabilistic graphical model.
The Hammersley-Clifford theorem specifically defines the necessary and sufficient conditions for a probability distribution to represent an undirected graphical model.
The concept of a clique is a fundamental graph-theoretic building block used to define the structure and factorization of undirected graphical models.
A maximal clique is defined as a specific type of clique that cannot be further extended while maintaining complete connectivity.
A Markov chain is defined by its specific conditional independence structure, where variables are independent of their past given their immediate predecessor.
Loopy BP applies the standard message-passing rules to graphs that contain cycles.
The intractability of exact computation due to large treewidth motivates the use of loopy BP as an approximation.
Loopy BP is a standard technique for inference in models like 2D Markov random fields.
Treewidth is a graph-theoretic property used to analyze the complexity of inference in graphical models.
Max-product BP is a variation of the standard BP message-passing rule where summation is replaced by argmax.
The max-product algorithm is specifically designed to compute the MAP estimate of hidden states.
BP reduces the cost of marginalization from exponential to linear in tree-structured graphs.
The complexity of inference is fundamentally tied to the treewidth of the underlying graph.
The belief propagation rule is derived by distributing marginalization sums over a tree-structured network.
The derivation specifically addresses graphical models with pairwise potentials, which are a form of undirected model.
The message-passing rule is the specific algorithm used to compute the belief propagation messages.
The rule is the operational result of the derivation process described in the preceding text.
In BP, the marginal probability at a node is computed as the product of all incoming messages.
The update sequence determines the order in which the BP message passing rule can be validly applied.
The Potts Model is used to define the compatibility matrices (pairwise potentials) in an undirected graphical model.
Messages are explicitly defined as the intermediate partial sums generated when performing marginalization over a graphical model.
The message passing formula utilizes potential functions (phi) which are defined as the factors of a Markov Random Field's joint distribution.
Comparing the two frameworks requires a prior understanding of what probabilistic graphical models represent.

overlay.rationale: Undirected graphical models are a specific type of probabilistic graphical model where edges lack directionality.
Directed and undirected models are the two primary types of graphical models, distinguished by how they factorize the joint probability distribution.
While MAP finds the mode of the posterior, MMSE finds the mean; they represent different strategies for penalizing estimation errors.
The factorization of a Markov chain's joint probability into functions of adjacent variables (cliques) is a direct application of the Hammersley-Clifford theorem.
The joint probability of an MRF factorizes into a product of functions over spatial neighbors, which are the cliques of the graph, as dictated by the theorem.
A Markov random field extends the one-dimensional linear dependency structure of a Markov chain into a two-dimensional spatial grid.
The Bethe free energy provides a variational objective whose minima correspond to the fixed points of the loopy BP algorithm.
This concept provides the formal mathematical definition for the messages introduced informally in the previous section.
The nosey neighbor rule provides an intuitive, anthropomorphic explanation for what a BP message represents.
Depth-first update is a specific schedule for ordering message updates in a tree-structured graph.
Parallel update is a synchronous schedule where every node sends messages simultaneously as soon as inputs are available.
Parallel and depth-first updates represent two different strategies for scheduling message passing in BP.
The Potts Model is frequently used as a prior for pixel disparity states in stereo vision applications.
